thread.title: The message investors are missing in the stock market’s wild swings: The economy is still solid

author: kopitiambot.com
title: The message investors are missing in the stock market’s wild swings: The economy is still solid
text:
(Source: marketwatch.com )
So now the Dow Jones Industrial Average soared 1,000 points in one day during a slow Christmas week, after falling sharply for four straight sessions. Is it OK to come out of the bunker?
Not really, if you’re thinking in the short term. Both the Dow
DJIA, +0.32%
and the S&P 500
SPX, +0.17%
are giving back a good chunk of Wednesday’s gain . The market’s heartburn naturally has refocused attention on the state of the economy — and it continues to be basically solid.
Yes, 2019 earnings growth looks a few percentage points weaker than it did a few months ago — S&P Capital IQ, for example, thinks corporate profits at S&P 500 companies will rise 6.8%, not the 10% it expected in September. But the signs of recession that everyone has been looking for aren’t really materializing.
“The economy is slowing, but so far it appears orderly,’’ said Ryan Sweet, director of real-time economics at Moody’s Analytics. “We call for GDP growth to slow in late 2019 and into 2020 ,… but do not forecast an outright recession.’’
Look at the data Moody’s monthly roundup of real-time economic indicators is pretty benign by the standards of the market’s recent sturm und drang, actually. Of the big economic drivers — consumer behavior, investment, inflation, housing and the labor market — it finds only investment acting like it’s late in an economic expansion and preparing for a downturn. One could quibble with its assessment that housing isn’t showing late-in-cycle behavior , but its take on the more-important labor market and consumer behavior seems accurate.
Here’s why.
• Early reports on Christmas suggest consumer spending is holding up — and consumer spending is still 70% of economic output. MasterCard reported that holiday spending growth was the best in six years , while Amazon.com said it had record unit sales , but didn’t disclose whether that meant big revenue gains
• Real-time crunching of the latest economic data from the New York and Atlanta Federal Reserve banks suggest that fourth-quarter growth kept up an annual rate of around 2.6%, which is still above the clip that most economists think is a sustainable, long-run average. U.S. growth will likely slow next year, but not disastrously, and not to any level below the 2.2% average we’ve seen annually from 2010 to 2017.
• Inflation is weakening, if anything, as oil prices
CLG9, -1.93%
plunge to $54 a barrel on international markets and about $45 for West Texas crude
CLG9, -1.93%
, down about 30% this year. Gasoline prices are under $2 a gallon in parts of the Midwest again, and futures prices point to a 2019 sag for natural gas that powers much of America’s heating and electricity.
• And while wage measures are improving, there’s still not much about them that points to overheating. The 3.1% wage gain workers got over the last 12 months is healthy, but not so healthy that it points to bidding wars that will soon be reversed. In fact, it’s still below peaks the U.S. saw in the late 1990s and mid-2000s, making Moody’s assessment that the economy is in mid-cycle, with little recession risk over the next year, perfectly defensible.
All of this moderates the risk, much spoken of lately, that the Federal Reserve will cause a recession by hiking interest rates too much too soon. The Fed can — and should — move slowly, and pause if hiccups in the data suggest higher rates are hurting consumers or hiring. Evidence, including the small changes in the central bank’s 2019 interest-rate guidance announced earlier this month, suggests that the Fed understands this just fine.
Read: Trump started a fight with the Fed he had zero chance of winning — now he’s backing down
What to do next Given that, the advice here is the same as it was one harrowing month ago — keep buying the way you always have, using the common-sense approach of dollar-cost averaging. Back in November, I explained that 401(k) warriors, and that’s most of us, are likely to be glad to own more $240 Tesla shares
TSLA, -3.02%
$135 Facebook shares
FB, +0.10%
and $175 Apple stock
AAPL, -0.82%
— probably as soon as next year.
Nothing I see changes any of that. There’s still no recession on the horizon, just a growth slowdown we all have known was coming. And electric cars, movie streaming, and other technology plays are still gradually uprooting the way we live. There’s nothing unfixable about Apple’s latest phone being too expensive for some customers, and some caution (but not panic) is warranted about how Facebook will adjust to U.S. policy makers’ focus on advertising and data privacy beginning probably in 2021 (the Trump administration is both too free-market and too unfocused to write significant new rules restricting online advertising).
If the stock market is in for a decade of torpor followed by another crash , true, this strategy won’t work. Nothing will.
But the best play is to bet on the genius of American capitalism — with a little extra focus on companies whose genius is a little more obvious than others. That plan worked just fine coming out of the 2000-2002 bust, the post-government shutdown bear market of 2011, and even through the pain of 2008 and its aftermath. It’s built for tougher times than these.
